The word flush as a verb has several distinct meanings, but many of them share an underlying idea: a sudden, forceful rush or surge — of water, blood, emotion, or action. Once you see that thread, the meanings start to feel connected.
1. To clean something by sending a rush of water through it

This is the most everyday meaning. When you flush something, you push a strong, sudden flow of water through it to clean it out or wash something away.

Examples:

  • You flush a toilet — you release a rush of water that clears out the bowl.
  • A doctor might flush a wound — pouring clean water into a cut to wash out dirt or bacteria.
  • A plumber might flush a pipe — sending water through it to clear a blockage.
  • You flush out your eyes after getting soap in them.

The idea is always the same: water comes in fast, sweeps everything clean, and carries it away.
2. To (cause to) turn red — especially the face

When blood rushes suddenly to your skin, your face flushes — it turns red or rosy. This happens because your blood vessels widen and more blood flows near the skin's surface.

Examples:

  • Her cheeks flushed when she heard the compliment.
  • His face flushed red after running up the stairs.
  • The fever made her skin flush.
  • He flushed with anger when he heard the insult.

Flush vs. Blush

These two words are very close, so it's worth knowing the difference:

  • Blush is almost always from an emotional cause — embarrassment, shyness, flattery. It has a softer, more intimate feel.
  • Flush is broader. It can happen from heat, exercise, fever, alcohol, drugs, or emotion. It often feels more physical and intense. A runner's face flushes — it doesn't blush.

Both describe redness in the face, but flush covers more ground.
3. To be "flushed with" something — overwhelmed by a strong feeling

This is a special pattern: flushed with [emotion or achievement]. It means to be suddenly and completely filled with a strong, usually positive, feeling — so much so that it shows outwardly.

Examples:

  • She was flushed with pride after winning the award.
  • The team came off the field flushed with victory.
  • He was flushed with excitement before the big day.

Think of it like this: the emotion is so intense, it "rushes through" you the same way water rushes through a pipe — it fills you up completely, and it shows on your face. The phrase is almost always positive (pride, success, victory, excitement), though rarely you might see it with something like flushed with shame.
4. To drive someone or something out of hiding

To flush out means to force a person, animal, or thing out of a place where they were hiding or concealed.

Examples:

  • Hunters flush birds from tall grass — they make noise or disturb the area until the birds suddenly fly up out of hiding.
  • Police flushed out the suspect from the building.
  • The investigation flushed out the corrupt officials.
  • Journalists flushed out the truth that had been hidden for years.

The image here is similar to flushing a toilet or a pipe: you send something in (noise, pressure, force, investigation) and it drives whatever is hiding out into the open. The word is very common with the preposition "out" — flush out.
5. To clear out stored data (computing / technology)

In computing, to flush means to force all the data that has been temporarily stored (in a cache, a buffer, or memory) to be sent to its final destination and the temporary storage to be emptied.

Examples:

  • The program flushed the buffer before closing.
  • You should flush the DNS cache to fix the connection problem.
  • The developer flushed the cache to make the new changes appear on the website.

Computers often hold data temporarily in a fast-access space (called a buffer or cache) before writing it to a permanent place. Flushing pushes all of that data out and clears the space — just like flushing a toilet clears the bowl.
6. To make something level or even (less common)

As a verb, flush can mean to make a surface perfectly level with another surface — so there's no ridge, bump, or gap between them.

Examples:

  • The carpenter carefully flushed the two panels so they sat perfectly even.
  • The tiles were flushed against the wall with no gap visible.

You're more likely to see this as an adjective ("the door is flush with the wall") than as a verb, but the verb form does exist in carpentry, construction, and design contexts. The idea: two things brought so perfectly together that they form one smooth, unbroken surface.

Now that you've seen all the meanings, notice what they share:

Flushed with emotionFeeling rushes through you, filling you completely

• Flush a toilet / wound / pipe → clean by sending water through forcefully
  • Face flushes → turns red because blood rushes to the skin
  • Flushed with pride/victory → completely overwhelmed by a feeling
  • Flush out → drive someone or something out of hiding
  • Flush a cache/buffer → clear temporary storage by pushing data to its destination
  • Flush a surface → make it perfectly level with another

That's the full picture of flush as a verb — in all its forms.
